output.summary: Loyalty mobile app for a 22-shop bakery chain: points, rewards and push offers, replacing a paper stamp card. The tills are old with no API and some shops have unreliable internet. Marketing wants a first version for the anniversary campaign. The Grão Dourado coffee chain loyalty app (b008) is a very close match: paper stamp card, 35 stores, old registers with no API, points sent from an agent on store computers, and an anniversary campaign deadline. It took 760 hours / $70,000 against an estimate of 600 hours. This chain has fewer shops (22 vs 35), but the flaky internet and no-API tills are the main drivers of effort, so the range stays close to the past actual with a margin for the register integration risk.
open_questions: How will points be captured at the till: QR code scanned at the register, a cashier entering a code, or a tablet or device beside the till? What hardware is in each shop?
Are there store computers on which a small agent can be installed? What operating system versions are in use, and who supports them?
How unreliable is the internet in the affected shops, and is offline operation required for earning and redeeming points?
Which tills and models are in use, and can sales data be exported (file, printout, database)?
How many customers are expected in the first six months, and how many push notifications per month?
What is the anniversary campaign date, and what must be in the first version versus later releases?
What are the reward rules: points per purchase value or per visit, expiry, and fraud and duplicate-scan prevention?
Is a back office for campaigns, segmentation and redemption reporting needed? Who will operate it?
Are iOS and Android both required, and is cross-platform acceptable?
Are there privacy or consent requirements (GDPR, local law) for customer data and push marketing, including account deletion?
How much technical training do shop staff have, and is on-site rollout or training needed for 22 shops?

risks.description: Software installed on old store machines can overrun: different Windows versions and flaky internet forced an offline queue with retries, adding unplanned work. Here the tills have no API and some shops have unreliable internet, so this is the biggest cost driver. It should be a separate line in the estimate and prototyped early.

output.summary: Android app for rugged handheld scanners for a fulfilment centre with 40 pickers: pick lists from the warehouse management system API, route guidance, barcode verification of every item, and offline operation when wifi drops. The target is to reduce about 1.5% wrong orders. A past warehouse picking project (b012) matches almost exactly in features, API style and problem (60 pickers, about 2% wrong orders, offline mode, REST API). It was delivered in 690 hours against an estimate of 700. Because this brief has fewer pickers and the same core scope, the range is centered near that actual, with a buffer for unknowns about the WMS API, devices and route logic. The other source (fleet tracking) is not comparable and was not used.
open_questions: Which warehouse management system is used, what does its API offer (REST, SOAP), and is the API owner available and cooperative? Is there a test environment?
Which scanner models and Android versions are in use? Can we get devices from week one for testing?
How is the best route defined: simple shelf-location order, or a layout-aware algorithm (aisles, one-way paths, zones)? Is a warehouse map or location coding available?
Is a supervisor screen or picker productivity reporting in scope?
How should short picks, substitutions and damaged items be handled, and must they be written back to the WMS?
How long can scanners stay offline, and how should sync conflicts be handled (e.g. stock changes or a list reassigned while offline)?
Are batch, cluster or multi-order picking, or multiple pick lists per picker, required?
Is there a pilot plan (one aisle or zone first) and a target rollout date?
How are pickers identified and logged in on shared devices?
Do items have reliable barcodes, including multiple barcodes per SKU, or is some labelling work needed?
Is multi-language support needed for the pickers?

risks.description: Older Android versions on the scanners can restrict library choices and cost extra effort. Test on the real devices from the start.

citations.quote: The old Android version limited some libraries and cost about 30 hours.

risks.description: Offline mode is a core requirement and needs to be designed from the start, including sync when the connection returns. The comparable project planned it upfront and it worked.

citations.quote: Offline mode was planned from the start and worked.

risks.description: Integration quality depends on the WMS API and on its owner being cooperative. Delays or limits in the API would put the estimate at risk.

citations.quote: a clear process with a cooperative API owner is predictable; test on the real devices from week one

risks.description: Evidence of the error reduction is thin: the comparable pilot had only a short measurement period, so the benefit of cutting wrong orders from 1.5% should be measured with a clear baseline and pilot period.

citations.quote: wrong orders dropped in the pilot aisle, though we only had four weeks of data

risks.description: Picker adoption with 40 people depends on scan feedback speed and training; slow feedback would undermine the benefit.

citations.quote: Pickers adopted the app quickly because the scan feedback was fast

risks.description: A route optimization beyond shelf-location order, if required, would add scope beyond the reference project.

assumptions: Baseline is the actual 690 hours of the warehouse picking app (b012), which had the same core features: Android rugged scanners, WMS pick lists with route order, barcode verification and offline sync.
Low end assumes a smaller site (40 vs 60 pickers) and a clear, cooperative WMS API owner, as in b012.
High end adds about 20-25% for unknowns: a different WMS API, possible device or Android constraints (b012 lost about 30 hours), and richer route logic.
Assumes route order is based on shelf location, not a layout-aware optimization algorithm.
Assumes the supervisor screen is in scope, as in b012; removing it would lower the range.
Excludes scanner hardware, device management and ongoing support.

citations.quote: Delivered in 690 hours against an estimate of 700, on target.
Works offline in dead zones of the warehouse and syncs when connected.

insufficient_info: The WMS vendor, API quality and scanner models in the new brief are unknown, so integration and device effort is uncertain.

sources.text: A distribution center with 60 pickers prepares orders using printed lists, and mistakes in picking cause about 2% of orders to be wrong. The operations manager wants handheld scanners with an app that guides each picker and verifies each item by barcode.

output.summary: Online small business loan application system for a credit union: applicant portal with document upload, analyst workspace with checklist and four-eyes approval, credit bureau query, and a full audit trail for the regulator. The client wants the analyst workflow live before the applicant portal. One past project (b014, loan application workflow for a regional credit cooperative) matches almost point for point, including the two-phase launch. It took 1,600 hours / $155,000 against an estimate of 1,300 hours, so the range is anchored on the actual outcome rather than the original estimate. Other sources (b010 wholesale portal) are only loosely related and were not used for the estimate.
open_questions: Has the credit bureau been chosen and is the access contract signed? Is a sandbox or test environment available now?
Which regulator and which audit, data retention and record-keeping rules apply? Is there a legal or compliance review of each screen or flow?
What does the credit checklist and scoring sheet look like, and is scoring manual or automated?
How should the four-eyes approval work: single approver pair, approval tiers by loan amount, rules for rejections and escalations?
How many analysts, applicants and applications per month are expected? How large are the uploaded documents, and are there malware scanning or retention requirements?
Which systems must the platform connect to (core banking, loan management, identity or e-signature)? Is any existing data to be migrated?
How should applicants and analysts authenticate (SSO, MFA)?
What reports are needed for management and for the regulator, and in what format?
What are the target dates for the analyst workflow and for the applicant portal? Is the phased launch fixed?
Where must data be hosted (in-country, specific cloud, on-premise)?

output.summary: Web streaming subscription service for an educational film publisher: about 600 hours of video, some with regional licensing limits, content protection demanded by rights holders, payments with trials and coupons, subtitle management and basic analytics, with an already announced festival launch. A past video subscription site (b023) matches almost feature for feature, including the festival deadline. It took 1,450 hours / $137,000 against an estimate of 1,000 hours. The main overrun drivers were DRM requirements that forced a change of video platform, library conversion and subtitle fixing. The new library is smaller (600 vs 800 hours), so the range is slightly below the b023 actual, but with a wide upper bound because DRM and licensing requirements are not yet confirmed.
open_questions: What DRM level or content protection do the rights holders require, and is it confirmed in writing? This must be settled before choosing the video platform.
Which countries are licensed for which titles, and are restrictions per title, per country, or both?
In what formats is the 600-hour library today, and who will convert and quality-check it?
How complete are the existing subtitles, in how many languages, and who produces missing ones?
Is the festival date fixed, and what minimum catalog and features must be live on that date? Is a reduced-catalog launch acceptable?
How many subscribers are expected in the first year, and what peak concurrent viewing is expected (affects streaming and delivery cost)?
Which payment provider, currencies and tax/VAT rules apply? Are annual plans, gift codes or multiple plans needed?
Which analytics are needed beyond views and churn, and do rights holders require viewing reports?
Does the editorial team need a CMS with roles, scheduling and metadata, or only basic uploads?
Which devices are needed (web only, or also TV and mobile apps)? The brief mentions web only.

output.summary: Internal document search for a consultancy: years of proposals and contracts (PDF and Word) on shared drives, searchable by meaning and keywords, with filters, passage highlighting, strict per-engagement access control, and no data leaving the client's cloud account. The law firm contract search project (b025) is a very close match in features and constraints. It took 700 hours / $66,000 against an estimate of 600 hours. Its overrun came from OCR on scanned PDFs and from a permission model that needed cleanup of the matter structure. The new brief does not state the document volume or the number of users, so the range is built on the b025 actual with room for OCR and access-control effort. Other sources (loan workflow, property portal) are not comparable and were not used.
open_questions: How many documents and how many years of material need to be ingested? What share is scanned PDFs needing OCR?
How are engagements structured today (folders, a CRM, a document management system), and is that structure complete and consistent enough to drive access rules?
How many users will search, and do they authenticate through an existing identity provider (e.g. Entra ID, Okta)?
Which cloud provider and services are allowed in the account? Are managed AI/embedding services permitted, or must models be self-hosted inside the account?
Which filters are needed (client, year, document type, author, engagement)?
Do access rules change over time (staff joining or leaving engagements), and must access be audited?
Are there confidentiality or client-contract restrictions on which documents can be indexed at all?
How will search quality be judged? Is there a set of known queries and expected results for a pilot evaluation?
Are documents in several languages?
What is the target launch date, and should the first release cover a subset of engagements?

citations.quote: Text extraction from scanned PDFs needed OCR and was messier than expected, around 70 hours more.

citations.quote: Delivered in 700 hours against an estimate of 600.

assumptions: Baseline is the actual 700 hours of the law firm contract search (b025), which had the same core features and the same cloud-account constraint.

High end adds about 35% over the baseline for more OCR work, cleanup of engagement and permission data, proposals needing different splitting rules, and a formal search-quality evaluation.

sources.text: A regional credit cooperative processes small business loan applications on paper and email. Approval takes two weeks. The board wants an online application with document upload, credit analysis workflow and a decision trail that the regulator can audit.
sources.title: Loan application workflow

sources.text:
- Applicant portal: application form, document upload, status tracking.
- Analyst workspace: checklist, scoring sheet, comments and four-eye approval.
- Integration with a credit bureau API.
- Full audit log of every action and decision.
- Reports for management and for the regulator.
sources.title: Loan application workflow

sources.text: Delivered in 760 hours against an estimate of 600. The mobile app was quick. The register agent was the problem: store computers had different Windows versions and flaky internet, and we had to build an offline queue that retried sending points. That alone was around 110 hours not in the estimate. Apple's review rejected the first submission over account deletion, a two-day delay. Lesson: any software installed on the client's old store machines needs its own line in the estimate.
sources.title: Loyalty app for a coffee chain

sources.text: Delivered in 1,600 hours against an estimate of 1,300. Audit and retention rules added roughly 150 hours: immutable logs, retention policies and a legal review of each screen. The credit bureau contract was delayed two months, so we built against a mock and found three format differences at the end. The internal workflow went live on time; the applicant portal slipped one month. Lesson: regulated domains need a compliance buffer of about 15 to 20 percent in our experience, but that figure comes from this single project.
sources.title: Loan application workflow

sources.text: Delivered in 700 hours against an estimate of 600. Text extraction from scanned PDFs needed OCR and was messier than expected, around 70 hours more. The permission model took longer because the matter structure had gaps that the firm had to clean. Search quality was judged good by the pilot group in informal tests, but we did not run a formal evaluation. Lesson: access control and document cleaning take more time than the search itself.
sources.title: Contract search for a law firm

output.summary: The client wants a modern, good-looking company website and asks for a cost. The brief gives no information about the type of site (brochure, ecommerce, portal), the number of pages, content, features, integrations or timeline. The past projects in the sources (property listing portal, video subscription site, shoe retailer migration, personal finance app, online course platform) are all complex, feature-heavy products and are not comparable to an unspecified company website. Any number drawn from them would be invented precision, so no estimate is given. The next step is a discovery conversation to define scope.
open_questions: What is the website for: presenting the company (brochure), generating leads, selling products online, or something else?
What does the company do, and who is the target audience?
How many pages or sections are expected, and is there a sitemap or a reference site the client likes?
Is there an existing website or domain? If so, should content and search ranking be migrated?
Who will write and supply the content, text, photos and branding (logo, colours, guidelines)? Is design work needed?
Which features are needed: contact forms, blog, booking, online payments, customer login, multiple languages?
Are there integrations with other tools (CRM, newsletter, analytics)?
Who will update the site after launch, and is a content management system needed?
Is there a budget range and a target launch date?
Are there accessibility, privacy or compliance requirements?
Who maintains hosting and support after launch?

risks.description: Without a defined scope, the cost can range from a small template-based site to a large custom build, so any quote given now would likely be wrong and could set a misleading expectation.
Subjective goals such as 'modern and good looking' are hard to verify and can cause design rework and disagreements over acceptance unless reference sites and approval steps are agreed.
Content (text, images, branding) is often delivered late by clients and can delay launch if responsibility is not agreed up front.

insufficient_info: The brief does not state the type of website, number of pages, features, integrations, content readiness or timeline.
None of the retrieved past projects is comparable to a general company website, so there are no actual hours or costs to base a range on.
No budget or deadline is given, so no estimate can be derived without inventing precision.

output.summary: Firmware for a satellite ground-station antenna controller: real-time motor control on a custom microcontroller board, radiation-tolerant design reviews and hardware-in-the-loop testing. None of the retrieved past projects involve embedded firmware, real-time motor control, custom hardware or radiation-tolerant design. They are web, mobile, data and integration projects (predictive maintenance, fleet dashboards, finance app, loyalty app, telemedicine). Their hours would not give a meaningful basis for this effort, so no estimate is given.
open_questions: Which microcontroller and board is used, and is the hardware design finished and available for firmware work, or still changing?
Which motors and axes are controlled (azimuth/elevation, stepper or servo), and what pointing accuracy, tracking speed and control-loop timing are needed?
Which RTOS or bare-metal framework and toolchain are expected, and is there existing firmware or a reference design?
What interfaces does the controller need (e.g. Ethernet, serial, CAN, encoders, limit switches, the ground-station software and its protocol)?
What radiation-tolerance requirements apply (total dose, single-event effects), and are the design reviews formal, with which standards (e.g. ECSS, NASA) and external reviewers?
What does hardware-in-the-loop testing involve: does a test rig or simulator already exist, or must it be built, and who provides the hardware?
Is this a ground-station antenna that is actually exposed to a radiation environment, or are the radiation-tolerant practices a design-quality requirement only?
What safety and fault-handling behaviour is required (e.g. emergency stop, watchdogs, fail-safe positions)?
What documentation, verification and traceability deliverables are expected?
What is the target delivery date, and how many prototype units and on-site test sessions are needed?

risks.description: No comparable past project exists, so any effort figure would be unsupported. Embedded real-time control, custom hardware and HIL testing are different in kind from the web, data and integration work in the sources.
Firmware work depends on custom hardware that may be late, unstable or revised, which blocks testing and causes rework. This comes from general judgment, not from the past projects.

Radiation-tolerant design reviews and formal verification can add substantial, hard-to-predict effort, and requirements may only emerge during reviews. A past project showed a similar pattern, where compliance reviews were revealed by the client after the first demo and caused an overrun.

citations.quote: compliance reviews of the prescription flow, which the client only revealed after the first demo

risks.description: Software that must run on or connect to client-specific devices and old machines tends to bring unplanned effort, such as retry and offline handling and device differences. Integration with the controller's interfaces may need its own estimate line.

citations.quote: any software installed on the client's old store machines needs its own line in the estimate

risks.description: Getting data or signals out of existing equipment can take far more effort than planned, as in the predictive maintenance project where data acquisition took about 500 hours. Sensor, encoder and protocol access on the antenna system could behave similarly.

citations.quote: Getting data out of the old controllers took about 500 hours: custom protocol adapters, network approvals and sensors that had to be installed.

insufficient_info: The sources contain no embedded firmware, real-time motor control, radiation-tolerant or hardware-in-the-loop projects, so no cited project is comparable and an hours or cost range would be invented precision.
Hardware platform, control requirements, applicable radiation standards and the HIL test setup are not described in the brief, so the effort cannot be sized.
A discovery or feasibility phase (hardware review, requirements and test-rig definition) would be needed before a reliable estimate can be given.

sources.text: Delivered in 1,900 hours against an estimate of 1,200, a large overrun. Getting data out of the old controllers took about 500 hours: custom protocol adapters, network approvals and sensors that had to be installed. Without labeled failures we could only build alert rules and simple anomaly detection, not a true failure predictor. The client accepted this after the pilot. Lesson: industrial data projects spend most of the effort on data acquisition, and the machine learning promise must be reduced when there are no labels.
sources.title: Predictive maintenance pipeline

sources.text: Delivered in 1,400 hours against an estimate of 1,100. The three vendor APIs behaved very differently: one had undocumented rate limits, one sent timestamps in local time without a timezone, and one changed its payload format once during the project. Normalizing the data into one model took about 200 hours more than planned. The real-time map was done within the first phase as expected. The fuel report was descoped halfway because one vendor did not expose fuel sensors. The client is happy with the map and the late-delivery alerts. Lesson: budget extra time for every external API, and ask for sample payloads before the estimate.
sources.title: Fleet tracking dashboards

sources.text: Delivered in 1,100 hours against an estimate of 900. Video itself was easy using a managed video API. The overrun came from the SAML integration (about 90 hours, the insurer's test environment was down for weeks) and from compliance reviews of the prescription flow, which the client only revealed after the first demo. Load tests showed the video provider's free tier was not enough, which changed the monthly cost for the client. Lesson: ask about compliance reviews and test environments before quoting.
